routes.description: Defend Catholic theism by reconciling uneven revelation, nonbelief, hell, inherited disorder, and suffering with universal grace, providence, and meaningful creaturely agency.
routes.successCriteria: Establish that God offers sufficient grace while differentiated circumstances, temporally extended revelation, free resistance, original sin, and formative suffering can explain apparent hiddenness without denying divine goodness.

motionBridge.description: Show that the disputed phenomena remain compatible with Catholic claims about universal grace, divine goodness, providence, and creaturely agency.

centralBridges.description: Explain how salvation and relationship with God remain genuinely available despite unequal cultural and evidential conditions.
Account for persistent nonbelief and damnation through meaningful creaturely resistance rather than divine refusal of relationship.
Connect original sin to present disorder without treating inherited deprivation as inherited personal guilt.
Explain how delayed disclosure and suffering can belong to a larger providential process of growing receptivity.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish gratuitous and differentiated divine gifts from an entitlement to identical temporal circumstances.
Supply theological and canonical interpretive principles for Genesis and Job rather than relying on isolated surface details.

routes.description: Argue that religious geography, sincere nonbelief, eternal consequences, inherited suffering, and unanswered suffering count against Catholic theism's account of divine love and providence.
routes.successCriteria: Establish that the observed distribution and persistence of nonbelief, together with morally arbitrary salvation conditions and inherited harms, are difficult to reconcile with a God able and willing to provide universal relationship and salvation.

motionBridge.description: Show that the disputed phenomena conflict with or are less expected under Catholic theism than under explanations without providential revelation.

centralBridges.description: Connect culturally patterned religious belief to a sociological explanation and challenge claims of universally accessible revelation.
Establish that sincere seekers can remain involuntarily unconvinced despite an alleged divine desire for relationship.
Show how contingent opportunities, cognitive limits, and eternal consequences create apparent arbitrariness or unfairness.
Challenge whether ancestral deception or refusal can justly explain deprivation and suffering borne by descendants.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Press the tension between providentially arranged conversion opportunities and the preservation of meaningful creaturely freedom.
Test formative interpretations of suffering against scriptural portrayals of divine conduct and compassion.

sections.title: Religious geography and fairness
sections.rationale: The accessibility and distribution of revelation directly bear on whether Catholic theism can reconcile universal salvific intent with unequal religious circumstances.

sections.title: Sincere nonbelief and salvation
sections.rationale: Whether conviction and salvation remain available to sincere seekers is central to the relationship among grace, cognitive limitation, freedom, and eternal consequences.

sections.title: Providence, contingency, and agency
sections.rationale: The debate requires an account of whether culturally mediated opportunities can be providential without making salvation arbitrary or compromising creaturely agency.

sections.title: Original sin and inherited deprivation
sections.rationale: Original sin supplies the Catholic explanation of disordered agency, while its initiating culpability and transmission determine whether present deprivation can be justified.

sections.title: Delayed revelation and formative suffering
sections.rationale: The personal case of sustained seeking and the dispute over Job test whether apparent silence and suffering can form receptivity within a loving providential order.
